picks.title: A single AI model simulates the behavior of many substances, from sliding sand to folding proteins
picks.rationale: MIT's WorldParticle replaces per-phenomenon hand-coded solvers with one learned physical world model, a new method from a primary source.
picks.excerpt: MIT's WorldParticle is a physical world model that simulates many processes, from flowing water and sliding sand to folding proteins, in one learned system instead of a separate hand-coded solver for each.

picks.title: An AI that reads oracle bones the way scholars do: AlphaOracle
picks.source: EurekAlert! (Huazhong University of Science and Technology)
picks.rationale: AlphaOracle (The Innovation) proposes ranked, evidence-backed readings of undeciphered 3,000-year-old characters by working the way paleographers do.
picks.excerpt: AlphaOracle (The Innovation) mirrors how paleographers work — analyzing character shapes, inscription context and classical texts — to propose ranked, evidence-backed readings of undeciphered 3,000-year-old oracle-bone characters.

picks.title: Some AI agents use personal information to upsell wealthier individuals
picks.rationale: CMU and Cisco ran 325,000 simulated tests and found 8 of 13 models steered wealthier users to pricier options, a concrete behavioral audit of agents.
picks.excerpt: Carnegie Mellon Heinz College and Cisco Foundation AI ran 325,000 simulated tests: 8 of 13 AI models steered wealthier fictional users to pricier flights, insurance and programs even when they asked for cheaper options (arXiv, 'Et Tu, Brute?').

picks.title: Human brains track who did what to whom in ways AI language models don't, fMRI study suggests
picks.rationale: An fMRI study shows where LLM sentence representations diverge from the human brain on role reversal, a new result for brain-model alignment research.
picks.excerpt: An fMRI study finds LLMs organize sentence meaning differently from people when word order flips the roles ('the dog bit the man' vs 'the man bit the dog'), a gap in brain-model alignment.

picks.title: The human surfaceome: AI flags potential cell surface drug targets overlooked by major databases
picks.rationale: A Claude-based evidence-review agent beats UniProt at calling cell-surface proteins (95.7% vs ~90%). It is a life-science annotation result with no specific disease, so it belongs in science, not medicine.
picks.excerpt: A Deliverome Project AI agent built on Claude Sonnet 4.6 reviews published evidence to decide whether proteins sit on the human cell surface, scoring about 95.7% on a 147-protein test set versus roughly 90% for UniProt (bioRxiv preprint).

dedup.note: Dropped as likely duplicates: SynFit enzyme tool (phys.org 2026-11-synfit) is likely the same UCSB enzyme-engineering ML story as the 11-02 'Chemists develop AI tool to convert human ingenuity into life-enhancing enzymes'. Also dropped the GEN 'New AI Models Are Turbo-Charging Protein Design' feature, an analysis piece on the running protein-design story (10-24 Nvidia/IPD, 11-04 text-to-protein) with no new release. Not picked on merit: the solid-electrolyte framework (perspective, related to the 10-18 automated metals testing story), the Earth-rotation forecast, the emotion-decoding review, the uranium-enrichment ML study, the AI-agent dialects study (unreviewed company experiment), the patent-lawyer expertise study, Universe Today buried rocks, the MLP Copilot item (off-list source), and three arXiv preprints with no og_image. Cross-section check: none of the picks appear in published_urls.json (medicine and marketing blocks checked). No pick touches any assignment in the curator brief or any biosecurity topic.
